newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Italy steps forward to EMU, Bonn staggers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy steps forward to EMU, Bonn staggers.

text.p: Italy stepped closer on paper to qualifying for the single European Union currency on Friday, while Germany openly aired doubts about its own ability to hit the budgetary target.
Italy, the country that "hard currency" advocates fear will slip into monetary union and weaken the new euro at birth, got a green light for a one-off tax to lower its budget deficit.
By contrast, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, whose country is the accepted core of economic and monetary union (EMU), said Bonn and others needed to do more to get their budgets in line.
Ernst Welteke, a member of the German Bundesbank, went further.

He told the Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper that Germany was unlikely to meet the three percent deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) target required for joining the first wave of monetary union in 1999.

But he said Bonn was likely be let in anyway, implying exactly the kind of interpretation of the rules that Germany has warned against in dealing with the EU's weaker economies, the so-called "Club Med" bloc of Italy, Spain and Portugal.

Europe's latest tango over the euro began in Brussels, where the European Commission's statistics agency, Eurostat, effectively said that Italy's accounting techniques for meeting EMU were above board.
It cleared Italy's eurotax, a one-off money raising measure designed to lower Italy's deficit in 1997, the budget year on which each country's fitness for joining the euro will be judged.
Eurostat said the Italian tax on wage funds was a new measure and could be recorded as reducing the deficit.

Although it only ruled on a portion of the proposed tax -- worth 0.19 percent of GDP -- European Commission officials stressed that the remaining portion was not in question. Hence, roughly 12.0 trillion lire ($7.2 billion), or about 0.6 percent of GDP, can now be applied towards the 1997 budget deficit.
In Rome, Prime Minister Romano Prodi made an aggressive speech to the Democratic Party of the Left, saying that a single currency without Italy was no single currency at all.
If the lira were not in the euro, it would be hammered by financial markets, he said, which would undermine Italy's economy and international standing.
"Europe is not just about a currency, it is impossible to think of Europe cut off from its great Latin culture," Prodi said. "German culture cannot represent by itself all of Europe."
He added that Italy, due to get a new mini-budget soon, was now within $3.6 billion to $8.4 billion of making the deficit criteria.
To the north, the mood was far less upbeat.

In a speech in Bonn, Kohl repeated the litany that there must be a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria if EMU was to work. Neither the timetable nor entry criteria for monetary union were open for renegotiation.
"We want a hard common currency," he said.
The Bundesbank's Welteke implied that by such standards, Germany might not make it.

"I share the doubts that the fiscal criteria will not be met this year, the reason behind that being the high unemployment rate and low tax revenues as well as higher government expenditures," he said in the newspaper interview.
Bonn officially says this year's deficit will be 2.9 percent of GDP, despite soaring unemployment levels that are straining the commitment to fiscal austerity.
But Welteke added that not hitting the three percent target should not close the door on Germany.
There was flexibility in the rules, he said, although countries that have not launched stability oriented policies should not be allowed in. ($ = 1663 Italian Lire)
